analysis.one_liner: Bars data brokers from selling or transferring people's location and health data.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in December 2024, sent to the Commerce Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that collect and resell information about individuals — to sell, share, or transfer a person's location data or health data, including searches for health services, pregnancy, mental health conditions, and diagnoses. The Federal Trade Commission would write the detailed rules, enforce the ban with civil penalties of up to 15% of a violator's parent company's annual revenue, and get $1 billion in funding to do the work. State attorneys general and private individuals could also sue violators. HIPAA-compliant health information handling, newsworthy publications, and disclosures a person explicitly authorizes would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose movements and health information are currently bought and sold — including people seeking abortion care, mental health treatment, or other sensitive services who could be tracked or targeted through their data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose health or location is tracked

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for data brokers to sell, license, trade, or transfer an individual's location data or health data, whether collected directly or inferred, including data about pregnancy, miscarriage, disability, and mental or physical health conditions.

Enforces the ban through the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits, with civil penalties of up to 15% of the violator's ultimate parent entity's revenue over the prior 12 months, and allows courts to order deletion of the data.
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC, available through fiscal year 2034, to carry out the law, and requires the FTC to issue its rule within 180 days so the ban takes effect quickly.
Protects data about specific groups of people who share a residence or IP address, not just named individuals, closing a common workaround used to sell neighborhood-level data.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the broader mobile-advertising ecosystem lose a lucrative market in location and health data. Taxpayers fund the $1 billion FTC appropriation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and location-data ad firms

drawbacks.text: The FTC must define key terms — including 'data' itself — through rulemaking within 180 days, so the ban's real-world reach depends heavily on how broadly the agency writes those rules.

The $1 billion appropriation to the FTC is a significant new federal expenditure, and the 15%-of-parent-revenue penalty cap is large enough that even supporters would acknowledge it could produce enormous single penalties against major companies.

The exemptions are narrow: only HIPAA-compliant handling, newsworthy publication, and explicitly authorized disclosures are permitted, which businesses that routinely share location or health-related data (such as app makers and retailers) would bear substantial compliance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, well-defined harm — the sale of people's location and health records — with strong enforcement tools and a large agency budget to back them. The main honest tradeoffs are the $1 billion price tag, very large potential penalties, and the fact that the ban's breadth depends on future FTC rulemaking. On its own terms it is a focused consumer-privacy measure rather than a sweeping regulation of all data collection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with under a month left in the Congress, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and died there when the session ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 10, 2024, joined by Sens. Sanders, Whitehouse, and Wyden, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action was taken before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It had three cosponsors and no recorded committee hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and location-data companies are better off; the ban never advanced, and nothing stops the existing trade in location and health data.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on December 10, 2024.

for.name: Sens. Bernie Sanders, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators signed on.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; the bill died in committee with no recorded Republican support and no recorded opposition vote.

industries.note: These companies' core business is collecting and reselling personal data, and the bill makes it unlawful for them to sell or transfer location and health data, with penalties up to 15% of parent-company revenue. Their revenue model depends on keeping that market open.

App and ad-tech companies monetize precise location and health-related signals through broker networks; the ban cuts off that resale channel, which would reduce a revenue stream built on tracking ordinary people's movements and health searches.
